title: Crowding density in urban environment and its effects on emotional responding of pedestrians: Using wearable device technology with sensors capturing proximity and psychophysiological emotion responses while walking in the street
authors: Anna Engelniederhammer, Georgios Papastefanou & Luyao Xiang, 2019
research_question: To examine the influence of crowding density in high-density urban areas on the emotional responses of people, specifically whether personal space invasions elicit aversive and/or appetitive emotional responses, measured in real-time using wearable sensor technology.

participants.description: Mean age = 24.77 (SD = 0.718), 68% female, Chinese people studying and living in Hong Kong for no longer than five years. Familiar with Hong Kong surroundings but still curious about the environment. No heavy mental illness history, no symptomatic systemic sweating, no accident events in the past month.
participants.recruitment: Subjects came to a predefined meeting point; specific recruitment method not detailed.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A predefined urban street walking path in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, a commercial center with very high pedestrian density. The path included four roads: Nathan Rd (street path 1), Peking Rd (street path 2), Hankow Rd (street path 3), and Haiphong Rd (street path 4). These varied in length and crowdedness.

measures.instrument: Electrodermal activity (EDA) and skin temperature, classified by a sensor wristband algorithm based on biopsychological emotion theory

mechanisms: High density leads to the invasion of personal space, which evokes emotional responses (stress, aggression, curiosity, interest).
Personal space is a phylogenetically acquired trait to prevent aggression.

Emotional responses are triggered by neuro-affective appraisal processes (automatic, non-deliberate, non-conscious matching of situational stimuli with prototypes like danger, reward expectation, novelty, loss).
implementation_implications: The accumulation of emotional responses from personal space invasions in crowded streets might contribute to overall stress load in high-density urban areas.
Future research could use body sensors to measure personal space and emotional responses to analyze urban antecedents of emotion effects.

limitations: Inability to uncover specific aspects of different street paths that elicit aversive or appetitive responses.
Sample is culturally specific (Chinese population in Hong Kong), limiting generalizability to other cultural contexts.
Reliance solely on objective psychophysiological data without additional self-report data, which could provide subjective labeling of emotions and crowding.
Sensor device unable to determine the entering direction of people into personal space.
